title: Cops ignored guidelines in jail death: Morency inquest expected to wrap up today
article: Windsor cops ignored their own prisoner care directives the day Craig James Morency died in their custody because they were too busy dealing with the fallout from drug raids and a murder investigation, a coroner's inquest heard Thursday.

Officers in the downtown detention centre were supposed to "physically inspect prisoners in their custody at least once every 30 minutes to confirm that each prisoner is breathing, not in distress and requires no further care," according to the directives.

But Morency, 36, who was felled by a morphine overdose in High Cell 6 about eight hours after his arrest inJune 2004, was left alone for more than two hours and slipped through the cracks on what police testified was an "unusual" and "hectic" day.
"He could have been laying in his bunk for a long time before it was noticed he was in distress," testified Dr. Margaret Thompson of the Ontario Regional Poison Information Centre in Toronto.
Tests showed Morency had 1,178 nanograms of morphine per millilitre of blood and Thompson estimated he ingested "at least" 10 or 12 60-milligram morphine pills or the equivalent amount of heroin.
She testified he likely swallowed a bag of pills so police wouldn't find his stash and died when the bag deteriorated in his stomach.
She stressed, under questioning from lawyer Craig Allen who is representing Morency's family, that police could have done little to save Morency once the drugs entered his body.
She said "he would have survived" if Morency told police he had swallowed the drugs and had been taken to hospital before the bag burst.
If police had kept him under close scrutiny similar to a suicide watch, "there is a higher likelihood he would have survived, but I can't say that he would have," she added when pressed.

The province's civilian agency that acts as a police watchdog absolved Windsor police in April of any wrongdoing in Morency's death after an "exhaustive investigation" involving six officers, including three forensic investigators.

Morency was arrested shortly after 7:30 a.m. June 22, 2004, at a Tim Hortons in the Wyandotte Street and Lauzon Road area after a witness phoned police saying he'd witnessed Morency rifle through a car in a nearby pharmacy parking lot.
He was frisked and placed in a prisoner's transport van with his hands cuffed behind his back.
But when he arrived at police headquarters, Morency's hands were cuffed in front of his body giving him access to his pockets.

Thompson said Morency probably swallowed the pills in the washroom at Tim Hortons but could have swallowed them in the transport van. She said it was "unlikely" he ingested the drugs in his cell because he knew he was to soon to be released on a promise to appear on the theft charge.
Special Const. Cathy MacDonald, now a data-entry clerk with Windsor police, found Morency unresponsive and covered with orange- coloured vomit when she delivered dinner to his cell about 4:35 p.m.

Morency seemed fine when he was fingerprinted about 2 p.m. but no officers checked on him again until MacDonald delivered his meal. He was rushed Hotel-Dieu Grace Hospital and pronounced dead about 5:40 p.m.
Special Const. Elaine LeBlanc started her shift along with MacDonald about 2:20 p.m., but didn't inspect the cell blocks as was customary because of the influx of prisoners.
"It was a very crazy day," she said.
"I never got a chance to walk around as soon as I came in."

Sgt. Wayne Beecroft testified it was too "hectic" to conduct the regular checks because investigators wanted strip searches done on suspects netted in drug raids and for those prisoners to be segregated from suspects detained in the murder investigation.
Police swooped down on 11 homes the day Morency died, arresting seven people, closing six grow operations and seizing an estimated $5.6 million in marijuana.
Detectives were also investigating the murder of 59-year-old Robert Phillips, who was killed June 11 in a house at 406 Glengarry Ave.
The coroner's jury will hear final submissions this morning and are expected to issue findings and any recommendations later today.
